title: SQL query detective
description: Read each query, predict what it returns, and spot the bug when the result is wrong. You'll work through joins, fan-out, NULL, aggregation, and filters that don't do what they seem to. Assume standard SQL unless a Question says otherwise. Without `ORDER BY`, row order doesn't matter.

questions.title: How many rows does this inner join return?
questions.description:
Tables:

- `customers`: `(1, 'Ada')`, `(2, 'Lin')`, `(3, 'Sam')`
- `orders`: `(101, 1)`, `(102, 1)`, `(103, 3)`, `(104, NULL)`

Columns are `customers(id, name)` and `orders(id, customer_id)`.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

Enter the number of result rows.
questions.explanation: Ada matches orders 101 and 102, and Sam matches 103. Lin has no orders, and order 104 has a NULL `customer_id`, so neither shows up. That's 3 rows.

questions.title: Which customer names does this query return?
questions.description:
Same `customers` and `orders` as before, but now each order has a `status`: 101 and 104 are `paid`, 102 and 103 are `pending`.

```sql
SELECT c.name
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
```

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join adds rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). Further cards note that a filter on the left table inside ON removes nothing, only preventing matches; that an inner join after a left join cannot match a NULL key, so authors without books vanish again; that counting only some children while keeping every parent means filtering in ON or pre-filtering the child in a subquery; and that LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.key IS NULL is a reliable anti-join only when that column is genuinely NOT NULL.
images.caption: Left panel: the NULL row the join adds fails the `WHERE` test.

questions.explanation: The `LEFT JOIN` keeps Lin with NULL order columns. Then `WHERE` drops that row, because `NULL = 'paid'` is unknown and `WHERE` keeps only true. Sam's only order is pending, so Sam goes too. Only Ada, with paid order 101, is left. With this filter, the left join behaves like an inner join.

questions.title: What does the query return with the paid filter moved into `ON`?
questions.description:
Same data as the previous Question.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND o.status = 'paid';
```

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join adds rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). Further cards note that a filter on the left table inside ON removes nothing, only preventing matches; that an inner join after a left join cannot match a NULL key, so authors without books vanish again; that counting only some children while keeping every parent means filtering in ON or pre-filtering the child in a subquery; and that LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.key IS NULL is a reliable anti-join only when that column is genuinely NOT NULL.
images.caption: Right panel: inside `ON`, the filter only decides which orders match.

questions.explanation: `ON` decides which orders count as a match, and a left join still keeps every customer. Ada matches paid order 101. Lin and Sam have no paid order, so their order columns are NULL. Order 104 has no customer, so it matches nobody.

questions.title: What are the counts for a customer with no orders?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS rows_seen, COUNT(o.id) AS orders_seen
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
```

Look at Lin, who has no orders.
questions.explanation: The left join gives Lin one row with NULL order columns. `COUNT(*)` counts rows, so `rows_seen` is 1. `COUNT(o.id)` skips NULLs, so `orders_seen` is 0.

questions.title: What `item_total` does this query report?
questions.description:
Order 10 has two items, priced 30 and 20, and three payments of 10 each.

```sql
SELECT SUM(i.price) AS item_total
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments AS p ON p.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.id = 10;
```

Enter the `item_total` it reports.

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing: 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times, then 20/10 three times. SUM(i.price) reports 150, counting each price once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, counting each payment once per item. A window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child. DISTINCT is not a fix, because it would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: Six rows, with each price counted once per payment.

questions.explanation: Each of the 2 items pairs with each of the 3 payments, so the joins produce `2 × 3 = 6` rows. Every item price shows up three times, and `SUM` returns `(30 + 20) × 3 = 150`. The real item total is 50.

questions.title: Which approaches give correct item and payment totals per order?
questions.description: Select every approach that works. Either child table can have two rows with the same amount.

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing: 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times, then 20/10 three times. SUM(i.price) reports 150, counting each price once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, counting each payment once per item. A window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child. DISTINCT is not a fix, because it would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: Reduce each child table to one row per order first.

options.text: Aggregate `order_items` and `payments` separately by `order_id`, then join the one-row-per-order results
Use a correlated scalar subquery per child table that aggregates it for the current order
Add `DISTINCT` to the final `SELECT` and keep both raw child joins

questions.explanation: Aggregate each child table before joining, or compute each total in its own correlated subquery. Either way, the child tables can't multiply each other. `SUM(DISTINCT amount)` breaks when two real rows have the same amount. A final `DISTINCT` comes too late, because `SUM` has already counted the duplicated rows.

questions.title: What does `NULL = NULL` evaluate to in a SQL predicate?

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: UNKNOWN, and a `WHERE` clause keeps only TRUE.

questions.explanation: It's unknown. NULL means the value is unknown, so SQL can't tell whether two NULLs are equal. A `WHERE` clause keeps only rows where the condition is true.

questions.title: Which standard SQL predicate treats two NULLs as equal?

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: The green card shows the standard predicate.

questions.explanation: `a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b` is true when `a` and `b` are equal or both NULL, and it never returns unknown. Plain `=` returns unknown if either side is NULL. Some databases also have their own NULL-safe operators.

questions.title: Which values does this `NOT IN` query return?
questions.description:
`candidate(id)` holds `1`, `2`, and `3`. `blocked(id)` holds `2` and `NULL`.

```sql
SELECT id
FROM candidate
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM blocked);
```

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: Written out with `AND`, the NULL comparison means no row can pass.

questions.explanation: `NOT IN` works like `id <> 2 AND id <> NULL`. For ids 1 and 3, the first part is true but the second is unknown, so the whole test is unknown. For id 2, the first part is false. `WHERE` keeps only true results, so the query returns no rows.

questions.title: Which values does this `NOT EXISTS` query return?
questions.description:
Same data: `candidate` holds `1`, `2`, `3`, and `blocked` holds `2`, `NULL`.

```sql
SELECT c.id
FROM candidate AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM blocked AS b
  WHERE b.id = c.id
);
```

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: `EXISTS` answers only yes or no, never unknown.

questions.explanation: The subquery finds a blocked row only for id 2. The NULL in `blocked.id` never equals a candidate id, so it doesn't affect anyone. Ids 1 and 3 pass `NOT EXISTS`.

questions.title: How many rows satisfy `rating <> 5`?
questions.description:
The `rating` values are `5`, `4`, and `NULL`.

```sql
SELECT * FROM reviews WHERE rating <> 5;
```

Enter the row count.

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: `<>` against NULL is UNKNOWN, so those rows never qualify.

questions.explanation: Only 4 makes `rating <> 5` true. 5 makes it false, and NULL makes it unknown. To include missing ratings, say so explicitly: `rating <> 5 OR rating IS NULL`.

questions.title: Which rows satisfy `COALESCE(discount, 0) = 0`?
questions.description: The `discount` values are `0`, `10`, and `NULL`.
questions.explanation: `COALESCE` returns its first non-NULL argument. A stored 0 stays 0 and NULL becomes 0, so both rows pass. Watch out: this treats 'no discount recorded' and 'a discount of zero' as the same thing.

questions.title: What does `SUM(amount)` return when no rows qualify?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT SUM(amount)
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'missing-status';
```

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: `SUM` of nothing is NULL, not zero.

questions.explanation: Without `GROUP BY`, an aggregate query always returns one row. `COUNT` of no rows is 0, but `SUM` and most other aggregates return NULL. Use `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)` when you want zero.

questions.title: What does `COUNT(amount)` return when no rows qualify?

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: `COUNT` of nothing is zero. It's the one aggregate that never returns NULL.

questions.explanation: Without `GROUP BY`, the query returns one row even when no rows qualify. `COUNT(amount)` counts non-NULL amounts, and there are none, so it returns 0.

questions.title: What is `AVG(score)` for scores `10`, `20`, and `NULL`?

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: The NULL is left out of both the sum and the count.

questions.explanation: `AVG` skips NULL, so it computes `(10 + 20) / 2 = 15`. If you count the missing score as zero, you get 10 instead. That's a different rule, and you have to write it out, for example as `AVG(COALESCE(score, 0))`.

questions.title: What is `COUNT(DISTINCT category)` for `A`, `A`, `B`, and `NULL`?

images.caption: NULL doesn't count as a distinct value here.

questions.explanation: The distinct non-NULL values are A and B. `COUNT(expression)` skips NULL, with or without `DISTINCT`, so the answer is 2.

questions.title: How many groups does `GROUP BY region` form?
questions.description: The `region` values are `'east'`, `'east'`, `NULL`, and `NULL`.

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: Grouping is the exception: all NULLs land in one group.

questions.explanation: `GROUP BY` puts both NULLs in one group, so you get an `east` group and a NULL group. That's different from plain equality, where `NULL = NULL` is unknown.

questions.title: Which customers does this query find?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT c.id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id
HAVING COUNT(o.id) = 0;
```

options.text: Customers with exactly one matching order
No customers, because a left join always makes `COUNT(*)` positive
Customers whose order ids are duplicated

questions.explanation: A customer with no orders still gets one row from the left join, with `o.id` set to NULL. `COUNT(o.id)` skips the NULL and returns 0, so `HAVING` keeps that customer. `COUNT(*)` would return 1, so it wouldn't work here.

questions.title: Why does this query leave out departments with no sales since the start of 2026?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT d.id, SUM(s.amount)
FROM departments AS d
LEFT JOIN sales AS s ON s.department_id = d.id
WHERE s.sold_at >= DATE '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY d.id;
```

options.text: The `WHERE` test rejects the NULL rows the left join added, before grouping
`SUM` automatically removes departments whose total is zero
`GROUP BY` cannot group rows produced by a left join
Date predicates are evaluated after aggregation

questions.explanation: The join runs before `WHERE`. A department with no sales since January 1 gets one row with `s.sold_at` set to NULL. The date test on that row is unknown, so `WHERE` drops it. Move the date condition into `ON` to keep every department.

questions.title: Which clause keeps only groups with total sales over 1,000?
questions.explanation: `WHERE` filters rows before the groups exist. `HAVING` filters the finished groups, so `HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000` is the right choice.

questions.title: What causes the duplicate matches?
questions.description:
A price is unique only by `(sku, region)`. Product `X` has one price for `US` and one for `EU`. You query an order line for `(X, US)` with:

```sql
SELECT l.sku, p.amount
FROM order_lines AS l
JOIN prices AS p ON p.sku = l.sku;
```

options.text: The join is missing `p.region = l.region`, which is part of the composite key
The price table needs a NULL row

questions.explanation: The join checks only `sku`, so the US order line matches both price rows. The full key is `(sku, region)`, so the join also needs `p.region = l.region`. Sorting the result won't remove the extra match.

questions.title: Which predicate produces each unordered employee pair exactly once?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT a.id, b.id
FROM employees AS a
JOIN employees AS b ON /* predicate */;
```

Employee ids are unique and non-NULL. Nobody should pair with themselves.
questions.explanation: `a.id < b.id` rules out self-pairs and keeps one ordering of each pair. `a.id <> b.id` gives you both `(a, b)` and `(b, a)`. `a.id <= b.id` also pairs every employee with themselves.

questions.title: How many rows does joining students through enrollments return?
questions.description:
Student 1 has 2 enrollments, student 2 has 3, and student 3 has none. Each enrollment points to one existing course.

```sql
SELECT s.id, c.id
FROM students AS s
JOIN enrollments AS e ON e.student_id = s.id
JOIN courses AS c ON c.id = e.course_id;
```

Enter the row count.
questions.explanation: Each enrollment links one student to one course, so each enrollment becomes one row: `2 + 3 = 5`. Student 3 has no enrollments and drops out of the inner join. Here 5 rows is correct, because the query asks for student-course pairs.

questions.title: A many-to-one join doubles some sales. What should you check?
questions.description: A sales fact table joins `stores` on `store_code`. Each sale should match one store, but some sales show up twice.

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing: 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times, then 20/10 three times. SUM(i.price) reports 150, counting each price once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, counting each payment once per item. A window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child. DISTINCT is not a fix, because it would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: A many-to-one join is many-to-one only if the right side is actually unique.

options.text: Whether the join leaves out part of the store's real key
Whether historical store versions need an effective-date condition
Whether a final `DISTINCT` makes the model correct

questions.explanation: If a sale matches two store rows, the join isn't many-to-one in practice. Look for duplicate `store_code` values, a missing part of the real key, or historical rows that need an effective-date condition. `DISTINCT` can hide some repeated rows, but it doesn't fix the relationship or a wrong total.

questions.title: Why is `SELECT DISTINCT` a risky fix for a join that duplicates rows?

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing: 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times, then 20/10 three times. SUM(i.price) reports 150, counting each price once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, counting each payment once per item. A window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child. DISTINCT is not a fix, because it would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: `DISTINCT` can't tell a duplicate from two items that cost the same.

options.text: It can hide the wrong join cardinality instead of fixing the join
It compares only the selected columns, so it can merge real records that look alike
It can't undo duplicates that an aggregate has already counted
It guarantees one output row per left-table key

questions.explanation: `DISTINCT` compares only the columns in the final result. Two real records can look identical there and get merged, while bad matches that differ in one column stay. It also can't fix `SUM(...)`, because the aggregate has already read the duplicated rows.

questions.title: Which rows can match because of missing parentheses?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM users AS u
JOIN events AS e
  ON e.user_id = u.id
 AND e.kind = 'purchase'
  OR e.kind = 'signup';
```

options.text: Every signup event can match every user, regardless of `user_id`
Signup events match only when `e.user_id = u.id`
No rows, because `AND` and `OR` cannot appear together in `ON`

questions.explanation: `AND` binds tighter than `OR`, so SQL reads the condition as `(e.user_id = u.id AND e.kind = 'purchase') OR e.kind = 'signup'`. Every signup event then matches every user. Parentheses fix it: `e.user_id = u.id AND (e.kind = 'purchase' OR e.kind = 'signup')`.

questions.title: How many rows does the full outer join return?
questions.description:
`a(k)` holds `1`, `2`, `2`. `b(k)` holds `2`, `2`, `3`.

```sql
SELECT a.k, b.k
FROM a
FULL OUTER JOIN b ON b.k = a.k;
```

Enter the row count.
questions.explanation: Both `a` rows with 2 match both `b` rows with 2, giving `2 × 2 = 4` rows. The unmatched 1 from `a` adds one row, and the unmatched 3 from `b` adds another. That's 6.

questions.title: How many rows do `UNION ALL` and `UNION` return?
questions.description: Query X returns `1, 1, 2`, and query Y returns `2, 3`. Compare `X UNION ALL Y` with `X UNION Y`.
questions.explanation: `UNION ALL` keeps every row: 3 from X plus 2 from Y makes 5. `UNION` removes duplicates, leaving 1, 2, and 3.

questions.title: How many rows does a cross join produce?
questions.description:
Table `sizes` has 4 rows and table `colors` has 6 rows.

```sql
SELECT * FROM sizes CROSS JOIN colors;
```
questions.explanation: A cross join pairs every size with every color: `4 × 6 = 24` rows. That's what you want when you need every combination, and a bug when you don't.

questions.title: Why do authors without books disappear from this join chain?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT a.name, p.name
FROM authors AS a
LEFT JOIN books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id
JOIN publishers AS p ON p.id = b.publisher_id;
```

With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). images.caption: The inner join that follows can't match a NULL key.

options.text: The inner join to `publishers` rejects the NULL book row
A left join cannot be followed by another join
The database evaluates the publisher join before the author join
Authors without books are grouped away

questions.explanation: The left join keeps an author with no books and sets the `b` columns to NULL. The inner join then checks `p.id = b.publisher_id`. No publisher matches NULL, so the author drops out. To keep authors without books, make the `publishers` join a left join too.

questions.title: Does a NULL join key match another NULL?
questions.description: Assume the join uses ordinary equality: `left.value = right.value`.

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: Two NULL keys compare as UNKNOWN, so they never join.

options.text: No; ordinary equality with NULL is unknown
Yes; joins automatically match NULL with NULL
Yes, but only in an inner join

questions.explanation: Join conditions follow the same NULL rules as any other condition. `NULL = NULL` is unknown, so the two rows don't match.

questions.title: Why does this window total show an inflated value?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT o.id,
       SUM(i.price) OVER (PARTITION BY o.id) AS item_total
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN shipments AS s ON s.order_id = o.id;
```

One order has 2 items and 3 shipments.

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing: 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times, then 20/10 three times. SUM(i.price) reports 150, counting each price once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, counting each payment once per item. A window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child. DISTINCT is not a fix, because it would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: The window sees the six duplicated rows instead of the two real ones.

options.text: The window function runs on the six joined rows, after the fan-out
Window functions always multiply sums by the number of tables
`PARTITION BY` performs a distinct aggregation first
The window frame excludes item rows

questions.explanation: The joins make `2 × 3 = 6` rows before the window function runs, so each item price appears three times, once per shipment. The window sum adds up all six rows and shows that inflated total on each one. Window functions keep every input row, so they can't undo fan-out.

questions.title: What does `SELECT id FROM tasks LIMIT 1` guarantee without `ORDER BY`?

options.text: At most one qualifying row, but not which row

questions.explanation: `LIMIT 1` guarantees at most one row, but not which one. Without `ORDER BY`, the database can return any matching row, and a different query plan may pick a different one.

questions.title: Which 2026 rows can this inclusive `BETWEEN` filter miss?
questions.description:
```sql
WHERE created_at BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
                     AND TIMESTAMP '2026-12-31 00:00:00'
```

options.text: Rows later than midnight on December 31, 2026
Rows exactly at midnight on December 31, 2026

questions.explanation: `BETWEEN` includes both ends, but the upper end is midnight at the start of December 31. Anything later that day is excluded. Use a half-open range instead: `created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00' AND created_at < TIMESTAMP '2027-01-01 00:00:00'`.

questions.title: Why does this expression count every row?
questions.description:
```sql
COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
```

options.text: `COUNT(expression)` counts both 1 and 0 because both are non-NULL
`CASE` cannot be used inside an aggregate
Zero is equivalent to NULL in SQL

questions.explanation: `COUNT(expression)` counts every non-NULL value. This `CASE` returns 1 or 0, never NULL, so every row counts. Drop `ELSE 0` so other rows return NULL, or use `SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

questions.title: What does `SUM(CASE WHEN paid THEN amount END)` return when no row is paid?

options.text: A syntax error because `ELSE` is mandatory

questions.explanation: Without `ELSE`, the `CASE` returns NULL for every unpaid row. If no row is paid, `SUM` sees only NULLs and returns NULL. Add `ELSE 0`, or wrap the sum in `COALESCE`, when you need zero.

questions.title: When is `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL` a reliable anti-join?

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join adds rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). Further cards note that a filter on the left table inside ON removes nothing, only preventing matches; that an inner join after a left join cannot match a NULL key, so authors without books vanish again; that counting only some children while keeping every parent means filtering in ON or pre-filtering the child in a subquery; and that LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.key IS NULL is a reliable anti-join only when that column is genuinely NOT NULL.
images.caption: Reliable only when that column can't be NULL on its own.

options.text: When the tested right-side column is never NULL on a real match
Whenever any nullable right-side column is tested
Only when the left table has no primary key
Only when both tables are empty

questions.explanation: An unmatched left row gets NULL in every right-side column. So test a column that's never NULL on a real match, such as a non-NULL key. If the column you test can be NULL, a real match can look unmatched.

questions.title: What happens when you put a left-table filter in `ON`?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT c.id, o.id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND c.active = TRUE;
```

Some customers are inactive.

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join adds rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). Further cards note that a filter on the left table inside ON removes nothing, only preventing matches; that an inner join after a left join cannot match a NULL key, so authors without books vanish again; that counting only some children while keeping every parent means filtering in ON or pre-filtering the child in a subquery; and that LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.key IS NULL is a reliable anti-join only when that column is genuinely NOT NULL.
images.caption: It blocks the match but keeps the row.

options.text: Inactive customers remain, but with NULL order columns
Inactive customers are removed from the result
The query is invalid because `ON` cannot reference the left table

questions.explanation: In a left join, `ON` decides which right rows match. It never removes left rows. An inactive customer fails the match but still shows up with NULL order columns. Put `c.active = TRUE` in `WHERE` to drop inactive customers.

questions.title: What's wrong with this query if you need one row per customer?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT c.id, o.id, SUM(i.amount)
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY c.id, o.id;
```

options.text: It returns one row per customer-order pair instead of one per customer
`SUM` cannot be used with two grouping columns
Grouping by an order id combines all customers
The joins must be cross joins for aggregation

questions.explanation: The `GROUP BY` columns set what each result row stands for. With `o.id` in there, you get one row per customer and order. Remove `o.id` from `SELECT` and `GROUP BY` to get one total per customer.

questions.title: Does a group containing only NULL scores pass `HAVING AVG(score) >= 0`?

options.text: No; `AVG(score)` is NULL and the comparison is unknown
Yes; an all-NULL average is zero
Yes; NULL is greater than every number
The aggregate query always throws an error

questions.explanation: `AVG` skips NULLs, and with no non-NULL scores the average is NULL. `NULL >= 0` is unknown, and `HAVING` keeps only groups where the condition is true, so this group is dropped.

questions.title: Which checks help find where unexpected fan-out begins?

options.text: Compare row counts and distinct business keys before and after each join
Group the candidate right-side key and inspect keys with `COUNT(*) > 1`
Temporarily select the join keys and duplicated entity ids for a small failing case

questions.title: Which query keeps every account but counts only successful logins?

With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join adds rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). options.text: `LEFT JOIN logins l ON l.account_id = a.id AND l.success = TRUE`, then `COUNT(l.id)`
`LEFT JOIN logins l ON l.account_id = a.id`, then `WHERE l.success = TRUE` and `COUNT(*)`
